mount-fuji.note: last eruption 1707-08; one of the Three Holy Mountains

easter-island.fact: The Rapa Nui people carved nearly 1,000 moai on this remote volcanic island between about 1100 and 1680 CE.
easter-island.note: was 'nearly 900 ... 13th to 16th centuries'; article: nearly 1,000 extant, carved 1100-1680 CE

mont-saint-michel.fact: Medieval pilgrims crossed the bay's tidal flats on foot, and the sands around this Normandy island still endanger walkers who skip the 2014 bridge.
mont-saint-michel.note: 'cut off at high tide' and 'faster than a person can run' unsupported; a bridge opened in 2014 and walkers on the sands face danger

neuschwanstein-castle.fact: Bavarian King Ludwig II began it in 1869 as a private retreat and died in 1886, years before it was finished.
neuschwanstein-castle.note: was 'built it in the 1860s'; built 1869 to 1892, Ludwig died 1886

serengeti-tanzania.fact: This Tanzanian ecosystem hosts one of the largest land animal migrations on Earth, a journey of about 800 kilometers.
serengeti-tanzania.note: was 'the largest ... roughly 1,000 km'; article: one of the largest, 800 km

galapagos-islands.note: Darwin's 1835 Beagle visit; studies inspired natural selection

dead-sea.fact: At about 440 meters below sea level, its shore is the lowest point on dry land on Earth.
dead-sea.note: was 'roughly 430 m'; article: 439.78 m below sea level as of 2025

hagia-sophia.fact: Completed in AD 537 as a Byzantine cathedral, it became the world's largest interior space and among the first to use a fully pendentive dome.
hagia-sophia.note: 'record for nearly a thousand years' unsupported; article supports largest interior space on completion

terracotta-army.note: found by well-digging farmers 1974; more than 8,000 soldiers

salar-de-uyuni.fact: This Bolivian flat covers over 10,000 square kilometers, and the brine beneath its salt crust is exceptionally rich in lithium.
salar-de-uyuni.note: 'half the world's known lithium reserves' contradicted (article: Bolivia about 22% of known resources)

lalibela-ethiopia.fact: According to tradition, Ethiopia's King Lalibela, who reigned about 1181 to 1221, ordered them built after a vision of Jerusalem.
lalibela-ethiopia.note: was '12th century'; his reign ran into the 13th; clue kept (scoriaceous basalt, 11 churches)

cappadocia-turkey.note: underground cities dug by Christians, cave churches, soft volcanic rock

plitvice-lakes.note: sixteen lakes; colours change with minerals, organisms, light, season

timbuktu-mali.note: 14th-century rise under Mali Empire, scholarship, thousands of manuscripts

socotra-island.note: a third of plant life found nowhere else

danakil-depression.note: 100 m below sea level; Erta Ale range

wadi-rum.note: Valley of the Moon; stood in for Mars (The Martian, Last Days on Mars)

richat-structure.note: 40 km; impact hypothesis rejected after 1960s studies

tristan-da-cunha.fact: This South Atlantic island, about 11 kilometers across, has a single settlement, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, named for a visiting British prince.
tristan-da-cunha.note: '2,400 km from the nearest other inhabited land' not in the article, and Gough Island (staffed weather station) is far closer

challenger-deep.note: deepest known point, nearly 11,000 m; 1,000+ atmospheres is general reference (about 1,086 bar)

alert-nunavut.fact: This Canadian Forces station sits just 817 kilometers from the North Pole, and the nearest Canadian city, Iqaluit, is 2,092 kilometers away.
alert-nunavut.note: 'closer to Russia's coast than to most of Canada' unsupported; article (Alert, Nunavut) gives Iqaluit 2,092 km

la-rinconada-peru.fact: This Peruvian gold-mining town sits at about 5,000 meters in the Andes, where the air holds about half the oxygen found at sea level.
la-rinconada-peru.note: was 'above 5,100 m'; article: 4,900 to 5,100 m, centre 5,000 m

bouvet-island.note: Queen Maud Land about 1,700 km south

topkapi-palace.fact: Its first court was known as the Court of the Janissaries, and its Privy Chamber keeps relics said to have belonged to the Prophet Muhammad.
topkapi-palace.note: 'Janissaries' bodies flung from the ramparts' unsupported; relics are in the Privy Chamber, not the harem

gyeongbokgung-palace.fact: Burned down in 1592 and rebuilt from 1865, the palace has staged a reenactment of the Joseon changing of the guard since 2002.
gyeongbokgung-palace.note: 'still recreates the 15th-century ritual' unsupported; reenactment began 2002

mount-everest-summit.fact: Its height of 8,848.86 m comes from a joint Nepalese and Chinese survey in 2020, after years of argument over whether to count the snow cap.
mount-everest-summit.note: 'Nepal's maps show 8,586 m ... world's 14th' fabricated (8,586 m is Kangchenjunga)

borobudur.fact: Built in the 8th to 9th century, it wraps 2,672 relief panels around nine stacked platforms, and it was abandoned around the time the Mataram capital moved east.
borobudur.note: 'work stopped in 1006 when the volcano erupted and buried the site' unsupported; article: capital moved to East Java between 928 and 1006, likely period of abandonment

leshan-giant-buddha.fact: Carved during the Tang dynasty and finished in 803, the figure has drainage channels hidden in its hair and body to carry rainwater away.
leshan-giant-buddha.note: 'cut between 1001 and 1153', the Song damming story and the stone umbrella are fabricated; built 712 to 803

ha-long-bay.fact: The bay's limestone towers have been shaped since the Miocene, and waves have cut notch caves with perfectly smooth, flat ceilings into their bases.

amber-fort-jaipur.fact: Amber Fort overlooks Maota Lake, and its Sukh Niwas was cooled by breezes blowing over a water cascade inside the palace.
amber-fort-jaipur.clue: Where does a hilltop fort near Jaipur hold a mirror palace that glittered in candlelight?
amber-fort-jaipur.note: 'one of the world's earliest formal gardens' unsupported; clue's '2,000 pieces of cut glass' unsupported (article: mirror mosaics, glittered under candlelight)

fushimi-inari-taisha.fact: Each of its roughly 10,000 torii was donated by a Japanese business, and about 800 of them stand in rows to form the tunnel-like Senbon Torii.
fushimi-inari-taisha.note: 'every gate from a company, which is why the tunnels never end' overstated; article: roughly 10,000 donated by businesses, 800 in the Senbon Torii

registan-samarkand.fact: The square's madrasas date from the 1400s to the 1600s, and the oldest was built from 1417 to 1420 by the astronomer-ruler Ulugh Beg.
registan-samarkand.note: observatory did not stand beside the square; year-length claim overstated

mogao-caves-dunhuang.fact: The Library Cave was walled up in the 11th century, and when it was found in 1900 it held up to 50,000 manuscripts.
mogao-caves-dunhuang.note: 'sealed for a thousand years when sand blew in' fabricated

potala-palace-lhasa.fact: The Fifth Dalai Lama began the present palace in 1645, and Chinese shells struck its windows during the 1959 Tibetan uprising.
potala-palace-lhasa.note: 'fired in 1959 and rebuilt from the walls' fabricated; clue kept (13 stories, 3,700 m)

mount-kinabalu.fact: At 4,095 m, Kinabalu's bare granite summit is one of the youngest granite intrusions exposed on Earth, and Pleistocene glaciers carved its slopes.

sigiriya.fact: The Lion Rock's frescoes of women survive near the Mirror Wall, where centuries-old graffiti speaks of 500 painted ladies.

bagan-myanmar.fact: Between the 11th and 13th centuries more than 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries rose on this plain, and the remains of over 2,300 survive.

darvaza-gas-crater.fact: Soviet engineers are said to have lit this collapsed gas field in 1971 to burn off poisonous gas; the pit is 60 to 70 m across and still burns.
darvaza-gas-crater.note: 'expecting it to burn out in weeks' unsupported; diameter 60 to 70 m

flaming-cliffs-bayanzag.fact: Roy Chapman Andrews named the orange sandstone cliffs of Bayanzag in the 1920s, and the site is most famous for the first discovery of dinosaur eggs.
flaming-cliffs-bayanzag.note: 'dinosaur skeletons in the 1920s' imprecise; known for first dinosaur eggs

lake-issyk-kul.fact: At 1,607 m in Kyrgyzstan's Tian Shan, this saline lake is 182 kilometers long and the eighth-deepest lake in the world.
lake-issyk-kul.clue: Where is the second-largest mountain lake in the world, which rarely freezes?
lake-issyk-kul.note: fact fabricated (6,248 m, more water than Baikal, drained by a king); clue said 'second-longest alpine lake ... never freezes'

gobekli-tepe.fact: Hunter-gatherers, not farmers, raised this hilltop of enclosures from around 9500 BC, which upset the idea that settled agriculture had to come first.
gobekli-tepe.note: deliberate burial claim dropped (not in the article, and disputed)

mohenjo-daro.fact: The Indus metropolis on this mound was one of the world's earliest major cities, and by about 1700 BCE it had been abandoned for reasons still debated.
mohenjo-daro.clue: Where is a brick-built, bitumen-lined Great Bath in a city built some 4,500 years ago?
mohenjo-daro.note: drains 'never needed repairs' fabricated; clue said the city 'vanished 4,500 years ago' (built c. 2500 BCE, abandoned c. 1700 BCE)

persepolis.fact: This ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid empire was burned by Alexander in 330 BC, and only its columns, stairways, doorways and parts of walls survived.
persepolis.clue: Where do stone reliefs of tribute bearers still climb the stairways of an empty royal terrace?
persepolis.note: 'survive almost intact' overstated; '23 subject nations' not in Persepolis or Apadana articles

nalanda-bihar.fact: This great monastery in Bihar drew scholars from across Asia, and its library supplied the Sanskrit texts that pilgrims like Xuanzang carried to East Asia.
nalanda-bihar.clue: Where did ancient India's most renowned Buddhist monastery teach monks from across Asia for centuries?
nalanda-bihar.note: clue's 'coin the decimal zero' and the al-Khwarizmi fact fabricated

fatehpur-sikri.fact: The Mughal emperor's capital is usually said to have been left when its water supply failed, and its Buland Darwaza gate towers 46 m over the city.
fatehpur-sikri.note: 'tallest gateway in the world' unsupported; water failure is the usual reason given

polonnaruwa-sri-lanka.fact: Sri Lanka's second ancient capital has the Galpota, a long stone inscription of King Nissanka Malla, and its ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
polonnaruwa-sri-lanka.clue: Where is a stone 'book' carved with a long inscription of King Nissanka Malla?
polonnaruwa-sri-lanka.note: lightning, toppling and elephant-shadow claims fabricated; '1,400 lines' and '8 m' not sourceable (Polonnaruwa, Nissanka Malla articles)

marco-polo-bridge.fact: Japanese troops demanded entry to the walled town of Wanping beside this Beijing bridge to search for a missing soldier, and the refusal led to fighting.
marco-polo-bridge.clue: Where did the opening shots of the Second Sino-Japanese War get fired in July 1937?
marco-polo-bridge.note: clue said August (incident was 7 July 1937); 'refused entry to the bridge' and guardhouse memorial wrong

son-doong-vietnam.fact: A local man found the entrance in 1990, but the largest known cave passage on Earth was not surveyed until a British expedition in 2009.
son-doong-vietnam.note: 1991 climber and Laos sinkhole fabricated; found by Ho Khanh 1990, BCRA expedition 2009

kharkhorin-mongolia.fact: Near this Orkhon valley town lie the ruins of Karakorum, which served for a short time as the Mongol Empire's capital under Ogedei Khan.
kharkhorin-mongolia.clue: Where are the ruins of the Mongol Empire's 13th-century capital, beside the Orkhon River?
kharkhorin-mongolia.note: fact (city raised from Buddhist sculptures, abandoned after one summer) and clue (built with bricks from its own temples) fabricated; Erdene Zuu was later built from Karakorum's ruins, not the reverse

dholavira-india.fact: Dholavira's excavators found a signboard about 3 m long bearing ten Indus script signs, at a city on Khadir Bet island in the Great Rann of Kutch.
dholavira-india.clue: Where did an Indus city on a desert island store its water in massive reservoirs?
dholavira-india.note: clue's 'older than Sumerian writing' false; water ring and Gulf of Kachchh location wrong (Great Rann of Kutch)

yolyn-am-mongolia.fact: This gorge in the Gurvan Saikhan Mountains once kept its ice field all year, but today the ice tends to disappear by September.
yolyn-am-mongolia.clue: Where does a narrow Gobi gorge named for the lammergeier hold an ice field several meters thick?
yolyn-am-mongolia.note: clue (tyrannosaur nest of 22 eggs) and fact ('Flaming Wall' fossils) describe the Flaming Cliffs, not this ice gorge; rewritten from the Yolyn Am article

ak-baital-pass.fact: At 4,655 m this pass in Tajikistan's Gorno-Badakhshan region is the highest point of the M41, the Pamir Highway.
ak-baital-pass.clue: Where does the Pamir Highway reach its highest point, in Tajikistan's high Pamirs?
ak-baital-pass.note: 'road from Kashgar to Dushanbe' wrong and winter ice cliffs unsupported; clue implied the pass is on the Tajik-Kyrgyz border (it lies inside Tajikistan)

lo-manthang-nepal.fact: This walled town was the capital of the Kingdom of Lo from its founding in 1380 by Ame Pal, and foreigners have been allowed in only since 1992.

lothal-india.fact: This Indus town in Gujarat's Bhal region was a planned township, and marine microfossils found in its dock show that sea water once filled it.
lothal-india.clue: Where did an Indus town build one of the world's earliest known docks?
lothal-india.note: bricks 'stamped with the year they were fired' fabricated; clue's 'world's oldest known port' contested (article: Wadi al-Jarf is older)

adams-bridge.fact: The 48 km chain of limestone shoals between India and Sri Lanka is, in the Ramayana, a bridge built by Rama's army to reach Lanka.
adams-bridge.note: was 80 km (article: 48 km); sonar survey claim fabricated

versailles-palace.fact: Versailles' Hall of Mirrors was added from 1678 to 1681, and in June 1919 the Treaty of Versailles ending the First World War was signed there.
versailles-palace.note: fountains running every day on Machine de Marly water unsupported; 357-mirror count not in the article

st-peters-basilica.fact: St Peter's dome rises 136.6 metres, and the basilica took 120 years to build, from 1506 until its dedication in 1626.
st-peters-basilica.note: 'second only to Florence's Duomo' false; 'four popes and nearly three centuries' false (1506 to 1626)

cologne-cathedral.note: 1248 to 1880 = 632 years; spires survived WWII bombing

brandenburg-gate.fact: Napoleon used the Brandenburg Gate for a triumphal procession in 1806 and took its Quadriga to Paris, but it came back to Berlin in 1814.

tower-of-london.fact: The Tower of London has served as a royal palace, armoury, treasury, menagerie and prison, and it still holds the Crown Jewels of England.
tower-of-london.note: ravens 'kept since the Wild Men' fabricated; 'palace for four centuries before becoming a prison' wrong (first prisoner by 1100)

st-basils-cathedral.fact: St Basil's was named after a holy fool and not after Basil the Great, and it was built from 1555 to 1561 to mark the capture of Kazan and Astrakhan.

acropolis-athens.fact: The Parthenon's columns swell subtly and its corner columns are slightly displaced, refinements built into the temple between 447 and 432 BC.
acropolis-athens.note: '2.4% thicker ... 2,400 years' precision unsupported; Parthenon article: entasis, displaced corner columns, 447 to 432 BC

sagrada-familia.fact: Construction of the Sagrada Familia began in 1882, and when Gaudi died in 1926 the basilica was only 15 to 25 percent complete.
sagrada-familia.note: plaster model photographed from an aeroplane fabricated

anne-frank-house.fact: Miep Gies and Bep Voskuijl saved Anne Frank's diary after the family's arrest in 1944, and it was published in 1947.
anne-frank-house.note: named the wrong people (Fritz Frank, Gies Huber) and year (1942); Miep Gies article

hungarian-parliament.fact: Designed by Imre Steindl in neo-Gothic style and opened in 1902, the building was chosen partly because it resembled London's Palace of Westminster.
hungarian-parliament.clue: Where does the neo-Gothic parliament with 691 rooms face the Danube?
hungarian-parliament.note: 'sited to stare back at the emperor's palace' unsupported; clue said 691 statues (the building has 691 rooms)

hermitage-museum.fact: The Hermitage grew from the 225 or 317 paintings Catherine the Great acquired from the merchant Gotzkowsky in 1764, and it opened to the public in 1852.
hermitage-museum.note: 'Dutch auctions' wrong (Gotzkowsky sale; sources give 225 or 317); 'no public entrance for decades' recast as opened 1852

wawel-castle.fact: Wawel Castle was the residence of Poland's kings for centuries, and a fire-breathing metal dragon now stands by the river below it.
wawel-castle.clue: Where did Poland's kings live for centuries in a castle on a hill above the Vistula?
wawel-castle.note: dragon breathes fire 'twice a day' unsupported; clue's 'a royal dynasty for five hundred years' wrong (several dynasties)

charles-bridge-prague.fact: Charles Bridge was the only way across the Vltava in Prague until 1841, and legend says its first stone was laid at 5:31 a.m. on 9 July 1357.
charles-bridge-prague.note: 'crowning saint is Saint Wenceslas' unsupported; 'five hundred years' overstated (1357 to 1841)

prague-astronomical-clock.fact: Prague's astronomical clock has run since 1410, when it was made by clockmaker Mikuláš of Kadaň and astronomer Jan Šindel.
prague-astronomical-clock.note: zodiac disc 'turns once for the 365 days' wrong

dubrovnik-city-walls.fact: Dubrovnik's walls run unbroken for about 1,940 metres around most of the old city and rise as high as 25 metres.
dubrovnik-city-walls.note: UNESCO 'three centuries' wording and '300 metres across' unsupported

bran-castle.fact: Bran Castle was built by the Saxons of Kronstadt from 1377, and it later served as a customs post on the pass between Transylvania and Wallachia.
bran-castle.note: was 'raised in 1378 ... as a customs post'; privilege 1377, customs role later

pompeii.fact: Pompeii's plaster casts were made by pouring plaster into the hollows that decomposed bodies left in the ash, a technique devised by Giuseppe Fiorelli.
pompeii.note: 'figures still frozen mid-stride stand in their shops' unsupported

hohensalzburg-fortress.fact: Construction of Hohensalzburg began in 1077 under Archbishop Gebhard, and later archbishops kept expanding it to protect their power.
hohensalzburg-fortress.clue: Where does one of Europe's largest medieval castles watch over the rooftops of Mozart's birthplace?
hohensalzburg-fortress.note: 'finished in 1077' wrong (begun 1077); bell legend fabricated; clue's '50 rooms' unsupported

matera-sassi.fact: Matera's Sassi grew from a prehistoric cave settlement, and in the 1950s the government moved most of their residents into new public housing.
matera-sassi.clue: Where were cave homes dug into a ravine's rock lived in from prehistory until the 1950s?
matera-sassi.note: cardinal's hat in a drop of water fabricated; clue's 'people still live ... trodden out of a tuff cliff' wrong (calcareous rock, residents relocated in the 1950s)

alberobello-trulli.fact: Alberobello's trulli were built of dry stone without mortar because the counts who owned the land from 1481 wanted homes that were easy to demolish.

ness-of-brodgar.fact: Activity at the Ness of Brodgar dates from around 3500 BC, and by 2200 BC the complex had been closed down and partly dismantled.
ness-of-brodgar.clue: Where in Orkney did a Neolithic complex of stone buildings stand between the Ring of Brodgar and the Stones of Stenness?
ness-of-brodgar.note: fact (dug in the 3100s BC, walled up, left to rot) fabricated; clue's 'dozen houses deliberately buried' unsupported

giants-causeway.note: about 40,000 basalt columns, 50 to 60 million years old; legend of a giant's causeway

blue-lagoon-iceland.fact: The Blue Lagoon is not a natural hot spring at all: its water is the runoff of the nearby Svartsengi geothermal power station.
blue-lagoon-iceland.note: 'kept hot so the plant's pipes never freeze' fabricated

strokkur-geyser.fact: Strokkur erupts every six to ten minutes, and the famous Geysir, a larger geyser that erupts far more rarely, lies just 50 metres to the north.
strokkur-geyser.note: Geysir 'erupted just once in modern times, for four days in 2018' fabricated

jokulsarlon-glacier-lagoon.fact: Jökulsárlón is fed by Breiðamerkurjökull, an outlet glacier of the Vatnajökull ice cap, whose blocks of ice about 30 m high calve into the lagoon.
jokulsarlon-glacier-lagoon.clue: Where do icebergs calve off a glacier into a lagoon and roll out to sea through its shallow mouth?
jokulsarlon-glacier-lagoon.note: 'bergs sink and resurface' unsupported; clue's 'within the hour' unsupported

kirkjufell-iceland.fact: Kirkjufell means Church Mountain, and it appeared in Game of Thrones as the arrowhead mountain seen north of the Wall.
kirkjufell-iceland.clue: Where does an arrowhead-shaped hill, said to be its country's most photographed mountain, rise on a peninsula's north coast?
kirkjufell-iceland.note: 'means misty mountain' false (Church Mountain); clue's 'little red church' unsupported

preikestolen-pulpit-rock.fact: Pulpit Rock is a steep cliff rising 604 metres above Lysefjorden, with an almost flat top about 25 metres square.

lake-bled.fact: Lake Bled surrounds a small island with a pilgrimage church, and since 1740 a few local families have held the right to row pilgrims across.
lake-bled.note: 'wade across ... since 1788' fabricated (oarsmen since 1740); 'only natural island' not in the article

mount-elbrus.fact: Elbrus tops out at 5,642 metres on its western summit, and its two dormant volcanic domes flank a saddle at 5,416 metres.

dettifoss.fact: Dettifoss is 100 metres wide and drops 44 metres into the Jökulsárgljúfur canyon on the glacier-fed Jökulsá á Fjöllum river.
dettifoss.clue: Where does one of Europe's most powerful waterfalls drop into a canyon of spray?
dettifoss.note: 'plunges 11 metres in two steps' wrong (44 m); clue's 'Europe's most powerful' (article: reputed second after the Rhine Falls)

loch-ness.fact: Loch Ness reaches 227 metres in depth, and the 1934 surgeon's photograph that fed the monster legend was exposed as a hoax using a toy submarine.
loch-ness.note: 'photograph of a flipper ... thought to be a duck' false; Loch Ness Monster article

auschwitz-birkenau.fact: Of the 1.3 million people sent to Auschwitz, 1.1 million were murdered, and from 1942 trains brought Jews from across Europe to Birkenau's gas chambers.

chernobyl-reactor-4.fact: In November 2016 a giant steel arch, the New Safe Confinement, was slid over Chernobyl's destroyed fourth reactor in a move that took 15 days.
chernobyl-reactor-4.note: '25,000-tonne ... single 36-hour operation' wrong (14 to 29 November 2016); New Safe Confinement article

stone-of-destiny.fact: Four Scottish students took the Stone of Destiny from Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1950, and since 2024 it has been on display in Perth Museum.
stone-of-destiny.note: 'English undergraduates ... from Scone Abbey' wrong; 'now sits in Edinburgh Castle' outdated (Perth Museum since March 2024)

malbork-castle.fact: Malbork Castle, built by the Teutonic Knights, was sold to King Casimir IV of Poland in 1457 and then served as a Polish royal residence until 1772.
malbork-castle.clue: Where did the Teutonic Knights build the largest castle in the world by land area?
malbork-castle.note: the known case: never dismantled or moved; clue's 'taken apart brick by brick and rebuilt 250 kilometres away' fabricated

newgrange.fact: Newgrange is aligned to the winter solstice sunrise, when light shines through the roof box above the entrance into the inner chamber.
newgrange.note: 'each December afternoon' wrong (sunrise); light no longer reaches the back wall

rock-of-cashel.fact: Legend says the rock landed here when St Patrick banished Satan from a cave in the Devil's Bit, a mountain 30 km to the north.
rock-of-cashel.clue: Where was Brian Boru crowned in 977, on a rock fortress a later king of Munster gave to the Church in 1101?
rock-of-cashel.note: legend garbled (devil exempting the town from hell); clue's 'kings crowned until 1101' and 'devil cracked' wrong

wartburg-castle.fact: In Wartburg Castle Martin Luther translated the New Testament from Greek into German in just ten weeks, while hiding there as Junker Jörg in 1521 and 1522.
wartburg-castle.note: 'about a fortnight' wrong (ten weeks); 'made him a fugitive' wrong (already hiding after Worms)

housesteads-hadrians-wall.fact: Housesteads was built in stone around AD 124, on top of the wall's foundations, after a change of plan added forts to Hadrian's Wall.
housesteads-hadrians-wall.note: 'garrisoned from about AD 122' wrong (wall begun 122, fort about 124); rampart silhouette claim unsupported

kizhi-pogost.fact: Kizhi's Church of the Transfiguration was built of wood with no nails except in its domes and roof, where about 180,000 nails hold 60,000 shingles.
kizhi-pogost.note: 'confirmed only in 1990 ... let them put some in' fabricated

brasilia-national-congress.note: Niemeyer design; dome and bowl chambers, twin towers

greek-theatre-of-taormina-d34-60.note: ancient Greek theatre, Etna view (stub but true)

hohenzollern-castle.fact: The present castle, the third on the site, was built between 1846 and 1867 as a family memorial, and none of the three German Emperors ever lived in it.
hohenzollern-castle.note: 'around 700 years old', Berlin evacuees and last emperor's residence all wrong

matterhorn-summit.fact: The first ascent in 1865, led by Edward Whymper, ended in tragedy when four of the seven climbers fell during the descent.

zugspitze-summit.fact: At 2,962 m it is Germany's highest mountain, and the Austrian border runs over its western summit, where a border checkpoint once stood.
zugspitze-summit.note: 'complete with a customs hut' outdated (checkpoint no longer staffed)

hallstatt.fact: Salt mined here since the Bronze Age funded the Hallstatt culture, and the ossuary at St Michael's Chapel holds more than 1,200 skulls, 600 of them painted.
hallstatt.note: '1847 ossuary with 6,000 skulls beneath the chapel' wrong (more than 1,200 skulls)
